case_info.scenario: A woman in her 30s undergoing peritoneal dialysis for kidney failure who was also being investigated for severe hyperparathyroidism presented with multiple skin lesions 1 day after undergoing cervical computed tomography with iodinated contrast. Physical examination revealed a polymorphous cutaneous eruption characterized by nodular vegetating lesions on the lower lip and right nasal ala (Figure 1A); papulovesicular lesions, either umbilicated or with an erosive center, clustered on the left cheek (Figure 1B); and 2 papulovesicular lesions with an erythematous-to-violaceous halo at the cannula insertion sites on the back of the right hand and the inner side of the wrist. The patient reported that the lesions were painful, with the ones in the oral mucosa impairing feeding. Additional symptoms included fever, fatigue, rhinorrhea, and odynophagia. Investigations revealed a negative COVID-19 polymerase chain reaction test, mildly raised inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein, 24.2 mg/dL), normal thyroid function test results, and a negative virology screen, including both polymerase chain reaction and IgM tests for herpes simplex virus type 1 and 2, varicella-zoster virus, and cytomegalovirus.
case_info.caption: Nodular vegetating lesions on the chin, lower lip, and right nasal ala (A), and papulovesicular lesions on the left hemiface (B).
case_info.explanation: Cutaneous biopsies of the vegetating lesion on the lip and 1 of the hand lesions showed a dense neutrophilic infiltrate on the reticular dermis with multiple foci of vasculitis, including marked fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel walls (Figure 2A). Multiple round mononucleated cells with an optically empty peripheral perinuclear halo were also identified (Figure 2B). Immunohistochemistry findings revealed diffuse positivity for myeloperoxidase that spared the round cells, which positive for the histiocytic marker CD163 and, focally, for CD3; CD20 was negative. Results of Ziehl-Neelsen and periodic acid–Schiff stains ruled out the presence of microorganisms. Clinical and pathological findings were in keeping with iododerma. The diagnosis was corroborated by a markedly raised serum iodine level (19 992 μg/L [normal range, 45-100 μg/L]). Complete resolution of skin lesions was possible with a combination of topical fusidic acid with betamethasone and oral corticosteroid 0.5 mg/kg/d tapered over 1 month. The patient’s fatigue and malaise also considerably improved. Iododerma is a rare type of halogenoderma that develops after exposure to iodine-containing compounds (eg, oral and intravenous iodinated contrast dyes, potassium iodide, amiodarone, topical wound care products). It mainly affects patients with kidney disease owing to impaired renal clearance and accumulation of iodine in the bloodstream.1,2Generally, it takes months of continuous exposure to a halogen (eg, oral iodine) to develop a halogenoderma. However, in the context of intravenous administration, cutaneous lesions can appear within 2 to 3 days (ranging from several hours to 8 days), especially in the context of kidney failure.1-3 Iododerma can present a diagnostic challenge. Clinically, lesions can progress rapidly and be polymorphous. However, the most common presentations are acneiform pustular eruptions1and vegetative plaques.2,4In extreme cases, patients can experience toxic effects and present with multiorgan involvement.2 Pathologically, a neutrophil-predominant inflammatory infiltrate is fairly unspecific and can be found in neutrophilic dermatoses such as Sweet syndrome and some infectious diseases.5In the present case, we also found histologic features that had recently been described in iododerma, namely a neutrophilic dermatosis with vasculitis and haloed structures simulatingCryptococcus.2Similarly to the 3 cases previously reported by Ko et al,5we showed that these cryptococcal-like structures were positive for a histiocytic marker and negative for myeloperoxidase. These structures in the setting of neutrophilic dermatosis should also be recognized as part of the histologic spectrum of iododerma. Knowledge of this histologic mimicker is important not only to facilitate the diagnosis, but also to avoid unnecessary antifungal medications.6 Pemphigus vegetans is a rare variant of pemphigus vulgaris with flaccid blisters that become erosions and can form fungoid vegetations in intertriginous areas, the face, and scalp. The characteristic tongue involvement and the presence of suprabasal acantholysis with positive immunofluorescence are distinct aspects.7Pyostomatitis vegetans is characterized by oral involvement with classic snail-track erosions, a strong association with inflammatory bowel disease, peripheral eosinophilia, and characteristic histological features (eg, intraepithelial abscesses with large amount of eosinophils).8Superficial granulomatous pyoderma is a rare variant of pyoderma gangrenosum with a more indolent course. However, facial involvement is particularly uncommon. A characteristic 3-layered granuloma is seen on histological findings.9 With the present case we want to highlight that, despite the diagnostic challenges, a history of exposure to iodine in the context of kidney disease with acute acneiform and/or vegetating lesions should raise the suspicion of iododerma. The diagnosis can be reiterated by histological findings of neutrophilic dermatosis with cryptococcal-like structures (with or without vasculitis), and confirmed by high serum or urine iodine levels. The main treatment of iododerma is to remove the trigger. In some cases, no additional therapy is required. In the case reported, the lesions healed completely with use of systemic corticosteroids, but cyclosporine and hemodialysis are possible alternatives.4

[Case]

Physical examination revealed a polymorphous cutaneous eruption characterized by nodular vegetating lesions on the lower lip and right nasal ala (Figure 1A); papulovesicular lesions, either umbilicated or with an erosive center, clustered on the left cheek (Figure 1B); and 2 papulovesicular lesions with an erythematous-to-violaceous halo at the cannula insertion sites on the back of the right hand and the inner side of the wrist. The patient reported that the lesions were painful, with the ones in the oral mucosa impairing feeding. Additional symptoms included fever, fatigue, rhinorrhea, and odynophagia. Investigations revealed a negative COVID-19 polymerase chain reaction test, mildly raised inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein, 24.2 mg/dL), normal thyroid function test results, and a negative virology screen, including both polymerase chain reaction and IgM tests for herpes simplex virus type 1 and 2, varicella-zoster virus, and cytomegalovirus.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 30s undergoing peritoneal dialysis for kidney failure who was also being investigated for severe hyperparathyroidism presented with multiple skin lesions 1 day after undergoing cervical computed tomography with iodinated contrast. Physical examination revealed a polymorphous cutaneous eruption characterized by nodular vegetating lesions on the lower lip and right nasal ala (Figure 1A); papulovesicular lesions, either umbilicated or with an erosive center, clustered on the left cheek (Figure 1B); and 2 papulovesicular lesions with an erythematous-to-violaceous halo at the cannula insertion sites on the back of the right hand and the inner side of the wrist. The patient reported that the lesions were painful, with the ones in the oral mucosa impairing feeding. Additional symptoms included fever, fatigue, rhinorrhea, and odynophagia. Investigations revealed a negative COVID-19 polymerase chain reaction test, mildly raised inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein, 24.2 mg/dL), normal thyroid function test results, and a negative virology screen, including both polymerase chain reaction and IgM tests for herpes simplex virus type 1 and 2, varicella-zoster virus, and cytomegalovirus.
case_info.caption: Nodular vegetating lesions on the chin, lower lip, and right nasal ala (A), and papulovesicular lesions on the left hemiface (B).
case_info.explanation: Cutaneous biopsies of the vegetating lesion on the lip and 1 of the hand lesions showed a dense neutrophilic infiltrate on the reticular dermis with multiple foci of vasculitis, including marked fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel walls (Figure 2A). Multiple round mononucleated cells with an optically empty peripheral perinuclear halo were also identified (Figure 2B). Immunohistochemistry findings revealed diffuse positivity for myeloperoxidase that spared the round cells, which positive for the histiocytic marker CD163 and, focally, for CD3; CD20 was negative. Results of Ziehl-Neelsen and periodic acid–Schiff stains ruled out the presence of microorganisms. Clinical and pathological findings were in keeping with iododerma. The diagnosis was corroborated by a markedly raised serum iodine level (19 992 μg/L [normal range, 45-100 μg/L]). Complete resolution of skin lesions was possible with a combination of topical fusidic acid with betamethasone and oral corticosteroid 0.5 mg/kg/d tapered over 1 month. The patient’s fatigue and malaise also considerably improved. Iododerma is a rare type of halogenoderma that develops after exposure to iodine-containing compounds (eg, oral and intravenous iodinated contrast dyes, potassium iodide, amiodarone, topical wound care products). It mainly affects patients with kidney disease owing to impaired renal clearance and accumulation of iodine in the bloodstream.1,2Generally, it takes months of continuous exposure to a halogen (eg, oral iodine) to develop a halogenoderma. However, in the context of intravenous administration, cutaneous lesions can appear within 2 to 3 days (ranging from several hours to 8 days), especially in the context of kidney failure.1-3 Iododerma can present a diagnostic challenge. Clinically, lesions can progress rapidly and be polymorphous. However, the most common presentations are acneiform pustular eruptions1and vegetative plaques.2,4In extreme cases, patients can experience toxic effects and present with multiorgan involvement.2 Pathologically, a neutrophil-predominant inflammatory infiltrate is fairly unspecific and can be found in neutrophilic dermatoses such as Sweet syndrome and some infectious diseases.5In the present case, we also found histologic features that had recently been described in iododerma, namely a neutrophilic dermatosis with vasculitis and haloed structures simulatingCryptococcus.2Similarly to the 3 cases previously reported by Ko et al,5we showed that these cryptococcal-like structures were positive for a histiocytic marker and negative for myeloperoxidase. These structures in the setting of neutrophilic dermatosis should also be recognized as part of the histologic spectrum of iododerma. Knowledge of this histologic mimicker is important not only to facilitate the diagnosis, but also to avoid unnecessary antifungal medications.6 Pemphigus vegetans is a rare variant of pemphigus vulgaris with flaccid blisters that become erosions and can form fungoid vegetations in intertriginous areas, the face, and scalp. The characteristic tongue involvement and the presence of suprabasal acantholysis with positive immunofluorescence are distinct aspects.7Pyostomatitis vegetans is characterized by oral involvement with classic snail-track erosions, a strong association with inflammatory bowel disease, peripheral eosinophilia, and characteristic histological features (eg, intraepithelial abscesses with large amount of eosinophils).8Superficial granulomatous pyoderma is a rare variant of pyoderma gangrenosum with a more indolent course. However, facial involvement is particularly uncommon. A characteristic 3-layered granuloma is seen on histological findings.9 With the present case we want to highlight that, despite the diagnostic challenges, a history of exposure to iodine in the context of kidney disease with acute acneiform and/or vegetating lesions should raise the suspicion of iododerma. The diagnosis can be reiterated by histological findings of neutrophilic dermatosis with cryptococcal-like structures (with or without vasculitis), and confirmed by high serum or urine iodine levels. The main treatment of iododerma is to remove the trigger. In some cases, no additional therapy is required. In the case reported, the lesions healed completely with use of systemic corticosteroids, but cyclosporine and hemodialysis are possible alternatives.4

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 30s undergoing peritoneal dialysis for kidney failure who was also being investigated for severe hyperparathyroidism presented with multiple skin lesions 1 day after undergoing cervical computed tomography with iodinated contrast. Physical examination revealed a polymorphous cutaneous eruption characterized by nodular vegetating lesions on the lower lip and right nasal ala (Figure 1A); papulovesicular lesions, either umbilicated or with an erosive center, clustered on the left cheek (Figure 1B); and 2 papulovesicular lesions with an erythematous-to-violaceous halo at the cannula insertion sites on the back of the right hand and the inner side of the wrist. The patient reported that the lesions were painful, with the ones in the oral mucosa impairing feeding. Additional symptoms included fever, fatigue, rhinorrhea, and odynophagia. Investigations revealed a negative COVID-19 polymerase chain reaction test, mildly raised inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein, 24.2 mg/dL), normal thyroid function test results, and a negative virology screen, including both polymerase chain reaction and IgM tests for herpes simplex virus type 1 and 2, varicella-zoster virus, and cytomegalovirus.
case_info.caption: Nodular vegetating lesions on the chin, lower lip, and right nasal ala (A), and papulovesicular lesions on the left hemiface (B).
case_info.explanation: Cutaneous biopsies of the vegetating lesion on the lip and 1 of the hand lesions showed a dense neutrophilic infiltrate on the reticular dermis with multiple foci of vasculitis, including marked fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel walls (Figure 2A). Multiple round mononucleated cells with an optically empty peripheral perinuclear halo were also identified (Figure 2B). Immunohistochemistry findings revealed diffuse positivity for myeloperoxidase that spared the round cells, which positive for the histiocytic marker CD163 and, focally, for CD3; CD20 was negative. Results of Ziehl-Neelsen and periodic acid–Schiff stains ruled out the presence of microorganisms. Clinical and pathological findings were in keeping with iododerma. The diagnosis was corroborated by a markedly raised serum iodine level (19 992 μg/L [normal range, 45-100 μg/L]). Complete resolution of skin lesions was possible with a combination of topical fusidic acid with betamethasone and oral corticosteroid 0.5 mg/kg/d tapered over 1 month. The patient’s fatigue and malaise also considerably improved. Iododerma is a rare type of halogenoderma that develops after exposure to iodine-containing compounds (eg, oral and intravenous iodinated contrast dyes, potassium iodide, amiodarone, topical wound care products). It mainly affects patients with kidney disease owing to impaired renal clearance and accumulation of iodine in the bloodstream.1,2Generally, it takes months of continuous exposure to a halogen (eg, oral iodine) to develop a halogenoderma. However, in the context of intravenous administration, cutaneous lesions can appear within 2 to 3 days (ranging from several hours to 8 days), especially in the context of kidney failure.1-3 Iododerma can present a diagnostic challenge. Clinically, lesions can progress rapidly and be polymorphous. However, the most common presentations are acneiform pustular eruptions1and vegetative plaques.2,4In extreme cases, patients can experience toxic effects and present with multiorgan involvement.2 Pathologically, a neutrophil-predominant inflammatory infiltrate is fairly unspecific and can be found in neutrophilic dermatoses such as Sweet syndrome and some infectious diseases.5In the present case, we also found histologic features that had recently been described in iododerma, namely a neutrophilic dermatosis with vasculitis and haloed structures simulatingCryptococcus.2Similarly to the 3 cases previously reported by Ko et al,5we showed that these cryptococcal-like structures were positive for a histiocytic marker and negative for myeloperoxidase. These structures in the setting of neutrophilic dermatosis should also be recognized as part of the histologic spectrum of iododerma. Knowledge of this histologic mimicker is important not only to facilitate the diagnosis, but also to avoid unnecessary antifungal medications.6 Pemphigus vegetans is a rare variant of pemphigus vulgaris with flaccid blisters that become erosions and can form fungoid vegetations in intertriginous areas, the face, and scalp. The characteristic tongue involvement and the presence of suprabasal acantholysis with positive immunofluorescence are distinct aspects.7Pyostomatitis vegetans is characterized by oral involvement with classic snail-track erosions, a strong association with inflammatory bowel disease, peripheral eosinophilia, and characteristic histological features (eg, intraepithelial abscesses with large amount of eosinophils).8Superficial granulomatous pyoderma is a rare variant of pyoderma gangrenosum with a more indolent course. However, facial involvement is particularly uncommon. A characteristic 3-layered granuloma is seen on histological findings.9 With the present case we want to highlight that, despite the diagnostic challenges, a history of exposure to iodine in the context of kidney disease with acute acneiform and/or vegetating lesions should raise the suspicion of iododerma. The diagnosis can be reiterated by histological findings of neutrophilic dermatosis with cryptococcal-like structures (with or without vasculitis), and confirmed by high serum or urine iodine levels. The main treatment of iododerma is to remove the trigger. In some cases, no additional therapy is required. In the case reported, the lesions healed completely with use of systemic corticosteroids, but cyclosporine and hemodialysis are possible alternatives.4

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 30s undergoing peritoneal dialysis for kidney failure who was also being investigated for severe hyperparathyroidism presented with multiple skin lesions 1 day after undergoing cervical computed tomography with iodinated contrast. Physical examination revealed a polymorphous cutaneous eruption characterized by nodular vegetating lesions on the lower lip and right nasal ala (Figure 1A); papulovesicular lesions, either umbilicated or with an erosive center, clustered on the left cheek (Figure 1B); and 2 papulovesicular lesions with an erythematous-to-violaceous halo at the cannula insertion sites on the back of the right hand and the inner side of the wrist. The patient reported that the lesions were painful, with the ones in the oral mucosa impairing feeding. Additional symptoms included fever, fatigue, rhinorrhea, and odynophagia. Investigations revealed a negative COVID-19 polymerase chain reaction test, mildly raised inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein, 24.2 mg/dL), normal thyroid function test results, and a negative virology screen, including both polymerase chain reaction and IgM tests for herpes simplex virus type 1 and 2, varicella-zoster virus, and cytomegalovirus.
case_info.caption: Nodular vegetating lesions on the chin, lower lip, and right nasal ala (A), and papulovesicular lesions on the left hemiface (B).
case_info.explanation: Cutaneous biopsies of the vegetating lesion on the lip and 1 of the hand lesions showed a dense neutrophilic infiltrate on the reticular dermis with multiple foci of vasculitis, including marked fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel walls (Figure 2A). Multiple round mononucleated cells with an optically empty peripheral perinuclear halo were also identified (Figure 2B). Immunohistochemistry findings revealed diffuse positivity for myeloperoxidase that spared the round cells, which positive for the histiocytic marker CD163 and, focally, for CD3; CD20 was negative. Results of Ziehl-Neelsen and periodic acid–Schiff stains ruled out the presence of microorganisms. Clinical and pathological findings were in keeping with iododerma. The diagnosis was corroborated by a markedly raised serum iodine level (19 992 μg/L [normal range, 45-100 μg/L]). Complete resolution of skin lesions was possible with a combination of topical fusidic acid with betamethasone and oral corticosteroid 0.5 mg/kg/d tapered over 1 month. The patient’s fatigue and malaise also considerably improved. Iododerma is a rare type of halogenoderma that develops after exposure to iodine-containing compounds (eg, oral and intravenous iodinated contrast dyes, potassium iodide, amiodarone, topical wound care products). It mainly affects patients with kidney disease owing to impaired renal clearance and accumulation of iodine in the bloodstream.1,2Generally, it takes months of continuous exposure to a halogen (eg, oral iodine) to develop a halogenoderma. However, in the context of intravenous administration, cutaneous lesions can appear within 2 to 3 days (ranging from several hours to 8 days), especially in the context of kidney failure.1-3 Iododerma can present a diagnostic challenge. Clinically, lesions can progress rapidly and be polymorphous. However, the most common presentations are acneiform pustular eruptions1and vegetative plaques.2,4In extreme cases, patients can experience toxic effects and present with multiorgan involvement.2 Pathologically, a neutrophil-predominant inflammatory infiltrate is fairly unspecific and can be found in neutrophilic dermatoses such as Sweet syndrome and some infectious diseases.5In the present case, we also found histologic features that had recently been described in iododerma, namely a neutrophilic dermatosis with vasculitis and haloed structures simulatingCryptococcus.2Similarly to the 3 cases previously reported by Ko et al,5we showed that these cryptococcal-like structures were positive for a histiocytic marker and negative for myeloperoxidase. These structures in the setting of neutrophilic dermatosis should also be recognized as part of the histologic spectrum of iododerma. Knowledge of this histologic mimicker is important not only to facilitate the diagnosis, but also to avoid unnecessary antifungal medications.6 Pemphigus vegetans is a rare variant of pemphigus vulgaris with flaccid blisters that become erosions and can form fungoid vegetations in intertriginous areas, the face, and scalp. The characteristic tongue involvement and the presence of suprabasal acantholysis with positive immunofluorescence are distinct aspects.7Pyostomatitis vegetans is characterized by oral involvement with classic snail-track erosions, a strong association with inflammatory bowel disease, peripheral eosinophilia, and characteristic histological features (eg, intraepithelial abscesses with large amount of eosinophils).8Superficial granulomatous pyoderma is a rare variant of pyoderma gangrenosum with a more indolent course. However, facial involvement is particularly uncommon. A characteristic 3-layered granuloma is seen on histological findings.9 With the present case we want to highlight that, despite the diagnostic challenges, a history of exposure to iodine in the context of kidney disease with acute acneiform and/or vegetating lesions should raise the suspicion of iododerma. The diagnosis can be reiterated by histological findings of neutrophilic dermatosis with cryptococcal-like structures (with or without vasculitis), and confirmed by high serum or urine iodine levels. The main treatment of iododerma is to remove the trigger. In some cases, no additional therapy is required. In the case reported, the lesions healed completely with use of systemic corticosteroids, but cyclosporine and hemodialysis are possible alternatives.4

Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

mistake -- keep them separate:

2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 30s undergoing peritoneal dialysis for kidney failure who was also being investigated for severe hyperparathyroidism presented with multiple skin lesions 1 day after undergoing cervical computed tomography with iodinated contrast. Physical examination revealed a polymorphous cutaneous eruption characterized by nodular vegetating lesions on the lower lip and right nasal ala (Figure 1A); papulovesicular lesions, either umbilicated or with an erosive center, clustered on the left cheek (Figure 1B); and 2 papulovesicular lesions with an erythematous-to-violaceous halo at the cannula insertion sites on the back of the right hand and the inner side of the wrist. The patient reported that the lesions were painful, with the ones in the oral mucosa impairing feeding. Additional symptoms included fever, fatigue, rhinorrhea, and odynophagia. Investigations revealed a negative COVID-19 polymerase chain reaction test, mildly raised inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein, 24.2 mg/dL), normal thyroid function test results, and a negative virology screen, including both polymerase chain reaction and IgM tests for herpes simplex virus type 1 and 2, varicella-zoster virus, and cytomegalovirus.
case_info.caption: Nodular vegetating lesions on the chin, lower lip, and right nasal ala (A), and papulovesicular lesions on the left hemiface (B).
case_info.explanation: Cutaneous biopsies of the vegetating lesion on the lip and 1 of the hand lesions showed a dense neutrophilic infiltrate on the reticular dermis with multiple foci of vasculitis, including marked fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel walls (Figure 2A). Multiple round mononucleated cells with an optically empty peripheral perinuclear halo were also identified (Figure 2B). Immunohistochemistry findings revealed diffuse positivity for myeloperoxidase that spared the round cells, which positive for the histiocytic marker CD163 and, focally, for CD3; CD20 was negative. Results of Ziehl-Neelsen and periodic acid–Schiff stains ruled out the presence of microorganisms. Clinical and pathological findings were in keeping with iododerma. The diagnosis was corroborated by a markedly raised serum iodine level (19 992 μg/L [normal range, 45-100 μg/L]). Complete resolution of skin lesions was possible with a combination of topical fusidic acid with betamethasone and oral corticosteroid 0.5 mg/kg/d tapered over 1 month. The patient’s fatigue and malaise also considerably improved. Iododerma is a rare type of halogenoderma that develops after exposure to iodine-containing compounds (eg, oral and intravenous iodinated contrast dyes, potassium iodide, amiodarone, topical wound care products). It mainly affects patients with kidney disease owing to impaired renal clearance and accumulation of iodine in the bloodstream.1,2Generally, it takes months of continuous exposure to a halogen (eg, oral iodine) to develop a halogenoderma. However, in the context of intravenous administration, cutaneous lesions can appear within 2 to 3 days (ranging from several hours to 8 days), especially in the context of kidney failure.1-3 Iododerma can present a diagnostic challenge. Clinically, lesions can progress rapidly and be polymorphous. However, the most common presentations are acneiform pustular eruptions1and vegetative plaques.2,4In extreme cases, patients can experience toxic effects and present with multiorgan involvement.2 Pathologically, a neutrophil-predominant inflammatory infiltrate is fairly unspecific and can be found in neutrophilic dermatoses such as Sweet syndrome and some infectious diseases.5In the present case, we also found histologic features that had recently been described in iododerma, namely a neutrophilic dermatosis with vasculitis and haloed structures simulatingCryptococcus.2Similarly to the 3 cases previously reported by Ko et al,5we showed that these cryptococcal-like structures were positive for a histiocytic marker and negative for myeloperoxidase. These structures in the setting of neutrophilic dermatosis should also be recognized as part of the histologic spectrum of iododerma. Knowledge of this histologic mimicker is important not only to facilitate the diagnosis, but also to avoid unnecessary antifungal medications.6 Pemphigus vegetans is a rare variant of pemphigus vulgaris with flaccid blisters that become erosions and can form fungoid vegetations in intertriginous areas, the face, and scalp. The characteristic tongue involvement and the presence of suprabasal acantholysis with positive immunofluorescence are distinct aspects.7Pyostomatitis vegetans is characterized by oral involvement with classic snail-track erosions, a strong association with inflammatory bowel disease, peripheral eosinophilia, and characteristic histological features (eg, intraepithelial abscesses with large amount of eosinophils).8Superficial granulomatous pyoderma is a rare variant of pyoderma gangrenosum with a more indolent course. However, facial involvement is particularly uncommon. A characteristic 3-layered granuloma is seen on histological findings.9 With the present case we want to highlight that, despite the diagnostic challenges, a history of exposure to iodine in the context of kidney disease with acute acneiform and/or vegetating lesions should raise the suspicion of iododerma. The diagnosis can be reiterated by histological findings of neutrophilic dermatosis with cryptococcal-like structures (with or without vasculitis), and confirmed by high serum or urine iodine levels. The main treatment of iododerma is to remove the trigger. In some cases, no additional therapy is required. In the case reported, the lesions healed completely with use of systemic corticosteroids, but cyclosporine and hemodialysis are possible alternatives.4

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before

       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.

       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.

       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."

   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.

   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule

       competing options already qualifies.

       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.

   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis

   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 30s undergoing peritoneal dialysis for kidney failure who was also being investigated for severe hyperparathyroidism presented with multiple skin lesions 1 day after undergoing cervical computed tomography with iodinated contrast. Physical examination revealed a polymorphous cutaneous eruption characterized by nodular vegetating lesions on the lower lip and right nasal ala (Figure 1A); papulovesicular lesions, either umbilicated or with an erosive center, clustered on the left cheek (Figure 1B); and 2 papulovesicular lesions with an erythematous-to-violaceous halo at the cannula insertion sites on the back of the right hand and the inner side of the wrist. The patient reported that the lesions were painful, with the ones in the oral mucosa impairing feeding. Additional symptoms included fever, fatigue, rhinorrhea, and odynophagia. Investigations revealed a negative COVID-19 polymerase chain reaction test, mildly raised inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein, 24.2 mg/dL), normal thyroid function test results, and a negative virology screen, including both polymerase chain reaction and IgM tests for herpes simplex virus type 1 and 2, varicella-zoster virus, and cytomegalovirus.
case_info.caption: Nodular vegetating lesions on the chin, lower lip, and right nasal ala (A), and papulovesicular lesions on the left hemiface (B).
case_info.explanation: Cutaneous biopsies of the vegetating lesion on the lip and 1 of the hand lesions showed a dense neutrophilic infiltrate on the reticular dermis with multiple foci of vasculitis, including marked fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel walls (Figure 2A). Multiple round mononucleated cells with an optically empty peripheral perinuclear halo were also identified (Figure 2B). Immunohistochemistry findings revealed diffuse positivity for myeloperoxidase that spared the round cells, which positive for the histiocytic marker CD163 and, focally, for CD3; CD20 was negative. Results of Ziehl-Neelsen and periodic acid–Schiff stains ruled out the presence of microorganisms. Clinical and pathological findings were in keeping with iododerma. The diagnosis was corroborated by a markedly raised serum iodine level (19 992 μg/L [normal range, 45-100 μg/L]). Complete resolution of skin lesions was possible with a combination of topical fusidic acid with betamethasone and oral corticosteroid 0.5 mg/kg/d tapered over 1 month. The patient’s fatigue and malaise also considerably improved. Iododerma is a rare type of halogenoderma that develops after exposure to iodine-containing compounds (eg, oral and intravenous iodinated contrast dyes, potassium iodide, amiodarone, topical wound care products). It mainly affects patients with kidney disease owing to impaired renal clearance and accumulation of iodine in the bloodstream.1,2Generally, it takes months of continuous exposure to a halogen (eg, oral iodine) to develop a halogenoderma. However, in the context of intravenous administration, cutaneous lesions can appear within 2 to 3 days (ranging from several hours to 8 days), especially in the context of kidney failure.1-3 Iododerma can present a diagnostic challenge. Clinically, lesions can progress rapidly and be polymorphous. However, the most common presentations are acneiform pustular eruptions1and vegetative plaques.2,4In extreme cases, patients can experience toxic effects and present with multiorgan involvement.2 Pathologically, a neutrophil-predominant inflammatory infiltrate is fairly unspecific and can be found in neutrophilic dermatoses such as Sweet syndrome and some infectious diseases.5In the present case, we also found histologic features that had recently been described in iododerma, namely a neutrophilic dermatosis with vasculitis and haloed structures simulatingCryptococcus.2Similarly to the 3 cases previously reported by Ko et al,5we showed that these cryptococcal-like structures were positive for a histiocytic marker and negative for myeloperoxidase. These structures in the setting of neutrophilic dermatosis should also be recognized as part of the histologic spectrum of iododerma. Knowledge of this histologic mimicker is important not only to facilitate the diagnosis, but also to avoid unnecessary antifungal medications.6 Pemphigus vegetans is a rare variant of pemphigus vulgaris with flaccid blisters that become erosions and can form fungoid vegetations in intertriginous areas, the face, and scalp. The characteristic tongue involvement and the presence of suprabasal acantholysis with positive immunofluorescence are distinct aspects.7Pyostomatitis vegetans is characterized by oral involvement with classic snail-track erosions, a strong association with inflammatory bowel disease, peripheral eosinophilia, and characteristic histological features (eg, intraepithelial abscesses with large amount of eosinophils).8Superficial granulomatous pyoderma is a rare variant of pyoderma gangrenosum with a more indolent course. However, facial involvement is particularly uncommon. A characteristic 3-layered granuloma is seen on histological findings.9 With the present case we want to highlight that, despite the diagnostic challenges, a history of exposure to iodine in the context of kidney disease with acute acneiform and/or vegetating lesions should raise the suspicion of iododerma. The diagnosis can be reiterated by histological findings of neutrophilic dermatosis with cryptococcal-like structures (with or without vasculitis), and confirmed by high serum or urine iodine levels. The main treatment of iododerma is to remove the trigger. In some cases, no additional therapy is required. In the case reported, the lesions healed completely with use of systemic corticosteroids, but cyclosporine and hemodialysis are possible alternatives.4

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 30s undergoing peritoneal dialysis for kidney failure who was also being investigated for severe hyperparathyroidism presented with multiple skin lesions 1 day after undergoing cervical computed tomography with iodinated contrast. Physical examination revealed a polymorphous cutaneous eruption characterized by nodular vegetating lesions on the lower lip and right nasal ala (Figure 1A); papulovesicular lesions, either umbilicated or with an erosive center, clustered on the left cheek (Figure 1B); and 2 papulovesicular lesions with an erythematous-to-violaceous halo at the cannula insertion sites on the back of the right hand and the inner side of the wrist. The patient reported that the lesions were painful, with the ones in the oral mucosa impairing feeding. Additional symptoms included fever, fatigue, rhinorrhea, and odynophagia. Investigations revealed a negative COVID-19 polymerase chain reaction test, mildly raised inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein, 24.2 mg/dL), normal thyroid function test results, and a negative virology screen, including both polymerase chain reaction and IgM tests for herpes simplex virus type 1 and 2, varicella-zoster virus, and cytomegalovirus.
case_info.caption: Nodular vegetating lesions on the chin, lower lip, and right nasal ala (A), and papulovesicular lesions on the left hemiface (B).
case_info.explanation: Cutaneous biopsies of the vegetating lesion on the lip and 1 of the hand lesions showed a dense neutrophilic infiltrate on the reticular dermis with multiple foci of vasculitis, including marked fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel walls (Figure 2A). Multiple round mononucleated cells with an optically empty peripheral perinuclear halo were also identified (Figure 2B). Immunohistochemistry findings revealed diffuse positivity for myeloperoxidase that spared the round cells, which positive for the histiocytic marker CD163 and, focally, for CD3; CD20 was negative. Results of Ziehl-Neelsen and periodic acid–Schiff stains ruled out the presence of microorganisms. Clinical and pathological findings were in keeping with iododerma. The diagnosis was corroborated by a markedly raised serum iodine level (19 992 μg/L [normal range, 45-100 μg/L]). Complete resolution of skin lesions was possible with a combination of topical fusidic acid with betamethasone and oral corticosteroid 0.5 mg/kg/d tapered over 1 month. The patient’s fatigue and malaise also considerably improved. Iododerma is a rare type of halogenoderma that develops after exposure to iodine-containing compounds (eg, oral and intravenous iodinated contrast dyes, potassium iodide, amiodarone, topical wound care products). It mainly affects patients with kidney disease owing to impaired renal clearance and accumulation of iodine in the bloodstream.1,2Generally, it takes months of continuous exposure to a halogen (eg, oral iodine) to develop a halogenoderma. However, in the context of intravenous administration, cutaneous lesions can appear within 2 to 3 days (ranging from several hours to 8 days), especially in the context of kidney failure.1-3 Iododerma can present a diagnostic challenge. Clinically, lesions can progress rapidly and be polymorphous. However, the most common presentations are acneiform pustular eruptions1and vegetative plaques.2,4In extreme cases, patients can experience toxic effects and present with multiorgan involvement.2 Pathologically, a neutrophil-predominant inflammatory infiltrate is fairly unspecific and can be found in neutrophilic dermatoses such as Sweet syndrome and some infectious diseases.5In the present case, we also found histologic features that had recently been described in iododerma, namely a neutrophilic dermatosis with vasculitis and haloed structures simulatingCryptococcus.2Similarly to the 3 cases previously reported by Ko et al,5we showed that these cryptococcal-like structures were positive for a histiocytic marker and negative for myeloperoxidase. These structures in the setting of neutrophilic dermatosis should also be recognized as part of the histologic spectrum of iododerma. Knowledge of this histologic mimicker is important not only to facilitate the diagnosis, but also to avoid unnecessary antifungal medications.6 Pemphigus vegetans is a rare variant of pemphigus vulgaris with flaccid blisters that become erosions and can form fungoid vegetations in intertriginous areas, the face, and scalp. The characteristic tongue involvement and the presence of suprabasal acantholysis with positive immunofluorescence are distinct aspects.7Pyostomatitis vegetans is characterized by oral involvement with classic snail-track erosions, a strong association with inflammatory bowel disease, peripheral eosinophilia, and characteristic histological features (eg, intraepithelial abscesses with large amount of eosinophils).8Superficial granulomatous pyoderma is a rare variant of pyoderma gangrenosum with a more indolent course. However, facial involvement is particularly uncommon. A characteristic 3-layered granuloma is seen on histological findings.9 With the present case we want to highlight that, despite the diagnostic challenges, a history of exposure to iodine in the context of kidney disease with acute acneiform and/or vegetating lesions should raise the suspicion of iododerma. The diagnosis can be reiterated by histological findings of neutrophilic dermatosis with cryptococcal-like structures (with or without vasculitis), and confirmed by high serum or urine iodine levels. The main treatment of iododerma is to remove the trigger. In some cases, no additional therapy is required. In the case reported, the lesions healed completely with use of systemic corticosteroids, but cyclosporine and hemodialysis are possible alternatives.4

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 30s undergoing peritoneal dialysis for kidney failure who was also being investigated for severe hyperparathyroidism presented with multiple skin lesions 1 day after undergoing cervical computed tomography with iodinated contrast. Physical examination revealed a polymorphous cutaneous eruption characterized by nodular vegetating lesions on the lower lip and right nasal ala (Figure 1A); papulovesicular lesions, either umbilicated or with an erosive center, clustered on the left cheek (Figure 1B); and 2 papulovesicular lesions with an erythematous-to-violaceous halo at the cannula insertion sites on the back of the right hand and the inner side of the wrist. The patient reported that the lesions were painful, with the ones in the oral mucosa impairing feeding. Additional symptoms included fever, fatigue, rhinorrhea, and odynophagia. Investigations revealed a negative COVID-19 polymerase chain reaction test, mildly raised inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein, 24.2 mg/dL), normal thyroid function test results, and a negative virology screen, including both polymerase chain reaction and IgM tests for herpes simplex virus type 1 and 2, varicella-zoster virus, and cytomegalovirus.
case_info.caption: Nodular vegetating lesions on the chin, lower lip, and right nasal ala (A), and papulovesicular lesions on the left hemiface (B).
case_info.explanation: Cutaneous biopsies of the vegetating lesion on the lip and 1 of the hand lesions showed a dense neutrophilic infiltrate on the reticular dermis with multiple foci of vasculitis, including marked fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel walls (Figure 2A). Multiple round mononucleated cells with an optically empty peripheral perinuclear halo were also identified (Figure 2B). Immunohistochemistry findings revealed diffuse positivity for myeloperoxidase that spared the round cells, which positive for the histiocytic marker CD163 and, focally, for CD3; CD20 was negative. Results of Ziehl-Neelsen and periodic acid–Schiff stains ruled out the presence of microorganisms. Clinical and pathological findings were in keeping with iododerma. The diagnosis was corroborated by a markedly raised serum iodine level (19 992 μg/L [normal range, 45-100 μg/L]). Complete resolution of skin lesions was possible with a combination of topical fusidic acid with betamethasone and oral corticosteroid 0.5 mg/kg/d tapered over 1 month. The patient’s fatigue and malaise also considerably improved. Iododerma is a rare type of halogenoderma that develops after exposure to iodine-containing compounds (eg, oral and intravenous iodinated contrast dyes, potassium iodide, amiodarone, topical wound care products). It mainly affects patients with kidney disease owing to impaired renal clearance and accumulation of iodine in the bloodstream.1,2Generally, it takes months of continuous exposure to a halogen (eg, oral iodine) to develop a halogenoderma. However, in the context of intravenous administration, cutaneous lesions can appear within 2 to 3 days (ranging from several hours to 8 days), especially in the context of kidney failure.1-3 Iododerma can present a diagnostic challenge. Clinically, lesions can progress rapidly and be polymorphous. However, the most common presentations are acneiform pustular eruptions1and vegetative plaques.2,4In extreme cases, patients can experience toxic effects and present with multiorgan involvement.2 Pathologically, a neutrophil-predominant inflammatory infiltrate is fairly unspecific and can be found in neutrophilic dermatoses such as Sweet syndrome and some infectious diseases.5In the present case, we also found histologic features that had recently been described in iododerma, namely a neutrophilic dermatosis with vasculitis and haloed structures simulatingCryptococcus.2Similarly to the 3 cases previously reported by Ko et al,5we showed that these cryptococcal-like structures were positive for a histiocytic marker and negative for myeloperoxidase. These structures in the setting of neutrophilic dermatosis should also be recognized as part of the histologic spectrum of iododerma. Knowledge of this histologic mimicker is important not only to facilitate the diagnosis, but also to avoid unnecessary antifungal medications.6 Pemphigus vegetans is a rare variant of pemphigus vulgaris with flaccid blisters that become erosions and can form fungoid vegetations in intertriginous areas, the face, and scalp. The characteristic tongue involvement and the presence of suprabasal acantholysis with positive immunofluorescence are distinct aspects.7Pyostomatitis vegetans is characterized by oral involvement with classic snail-track erosions, a strong association with inflammatory bowel disease, peripheral eosinophilia, and characteristic histological features (eg, intraepithelial abscesses with large amount of eosinophils).8Superficial granulomatous pyoderma is a rare variant of pyoderma gangrenosum with a more indolent course. However, facial involvement is particularly uncommon. A characteristic 3-layered granuloma is seen on histological findings.9 With the present case we want to highlight that, despite the diagnostic challenges, a history of exposure to iodine in the context of kidney disease with acute acneiform and/or vegetating lesions should raise the suspicion of iododerma. The diagnosis can be reiterated by histological findings of neutrophilic dermatosis with cryptococcal-like structures (with or without vasculitis), and confirmed by high serum or urine iodine levels. The main treatment of iododerma is to remove the trigger. In some cases, no additional therapy is required. In the case reported, the lesions healed completely with use of systemic corticosteroids, but cyclosporine and hemodialysis are possible alternatives.4
